analysis.one_liner: Guarantees mothers and newborns at least 48 hours of insurance-covered hospital care after birth.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care after vaginal birth and 96 after a cesarean drew 122 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a House vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health plans and employer health benefits that cover maternity to pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a normal vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, without requiring the mother's doctor to get the plan's permission first. If a mother and her doctor chose an earlier discharge, the plan would have to cover follow-up care, including a home visit by a nurse or other qualified provider. It also barred plans from pressuring mothers or doctors to leave early and protected stronger state laws. It never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: New mothers and their newborns covered by private health insurance. They would no longer face plans that push mother and baby out of the hospital within a day or two of birth to save money. Mothers who chose to go home early would get guaranteed follow-up care at home or in a clinic, and doctors could not be penalized for keeping a mother and baby in the hospital.

how_it_helps.text: Requires any health plan or employer plan covering maternity to pay for at least 48 hours of inpatient care after a vaginal delivery and 96 hours after a cesarean, with no prior authorization needed from the plan to stay that long.

If the mother and her attending provider choose to leave the hospital before the minimum stay, the plan must cover timely follow-up care — including the option of care in the home by a nurse, nurse practitioner, nurse midwife, physician assistant, or physician experienced in maternal and child health.

Bars plans from denying enrollment or coverage because of the law, from offering mothers money to leave early, from rewarding doctors for early discharge, and from cutting a provider's pay for keeping a mother and baby in the hospital.
Does not override state laws that already require the same or stronger minimum stays, so states that had acted first kept their protections.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that fund health benefits would bear the cost of added covered hospital days and follow-up visits, costs that in practice flow into premiums. Managed care plans would also lose the savings from discharging mothers within a day or two of birth.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers funding benefits

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds covered days of hospital care that insurers and employers pay for, and those costs are generally passed into premiums. The bill also sets a fixed day-count floor, even though its own findings say the length of care should depend on each mother's health, support at home, and access to follow-up care; the bill reconciles this only by letting the attending provider and mother agree to an earlier discharge if the plan covers follow-up care.

Enforcement is split and thin: states enforce the rules for insurance plans, self-funded employee benefit plans are enforced only through the limited remedies of the federal ERISA law, and the Secretary of Labor is barred from enforcing the standards directly unless a state fails to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits this was a modest, narrowly targeted protection with real value: it addressed a specific practice — discharging mothers and newborns within a day or two of birth to cut costs — with a clear standard, a genuine opt-out paired with guaranteed follow-up care, and room for stronger state laws. The added premium cost falls on insurers and employers rather than directly on families. The serious defect is not the design but the fate: it never got a vote, so mothers and newborns got none of these protections from this bill in this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House subcommittees, never got a markup or a vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

narrative.text: Representative Gerald B.H. Solomon, a Republican, introduced the bill on March 29, 1996 together with Representative George Miller, a California Democrat — an unusually bipartisan pairing for this kind of insurance mandate.
The Speaker referred it to two committees at once, Commerce and Economic and Educational Opportunities, splitting jurisdiction over health insurance and employer benefits.
In April 1996 it was sent to the Health and Environment subcommittee of Commerce and the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee of the other committee — the last recorded action.
It gathered 122 cosponsors, 81 Democrats, 39 Republicans, and 2 Independents, but no committee ever marked it up and the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans came out ahead, along with the employers who fund benefits: neither had to meet the minimum-stay requirement or pay for guaranteed follow-up care. New mothers and newborns got no federal protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoiding the mandate

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill would have ended the cost-saving practice of discharging mothers within a day or two of birth by requiring 48 to 96 covered hours without prior authorization, plus follow-up care for early discharges. Its savings came directly out of care for mothers and newborns.

Longer covered stays mean more paid inpatient days for maternity wards, and mothers and newborns get more time for recovery and monitoring. The home-visit option would have shifted some follow-up care out of the hospital.

The bill bars plans from cutting a provider's reimbursement for keeping a mother and baby in the hospital, and it places the discharge decision with the attending provider in consultation with the mother rather than with the plan.
